games.title: Alive, Not Alive, or Argue It!
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is a card game about tricky cases. Each card describes something puzzling. Players decide if it is alive, not alive, or something scientists still argue about, and give a reason.

printables.title: 20 mystery cards to cut out
items: A candle flame: I eat wax, I need air, I grow and I make new flames.
A salt crystal: I grow bigger every day in salty water.
A dry rajma seed: I have sat in a jar for a year doing nothing.
A water bear: I am a tiny animal. I can dry into a ball and wake years later.
A virus: I do nothing alone. Inside a cell, I make thousands of copies of me.
A toy robot: I walk, I beep, I sense your hand. I run on batteries.
A cloud: I grow, I move, I split into little clouds.
A mule: I eat, grow and breathe, but I can't have babies.
Your hair: I grow longer every week, but cutting me doesn't hurt.
A picked mango: I was taken off the tree. I am slowly ripening.
Dried yeast in a packet: I look like sand.
A river: I flow, I carve valleys, I am full of fish.
A wooden chair: I was once a tree.
A mushroom: I have no leaves and no mouth. I eat dead wood.
Curd: I am full of tiny bacteria.
A computer program that copies itself and changes a little each time.
A hen's egg from the shop, never sat on by a hen.
A lotus seed found in a dry lake bed, about 1,300 years old.
A tree stump, cut last year, with a green shoot growing from its side.
A xenobot: a tiny blob built by scientists from frog cells. It swims.

printables.title: 9 sign cards to keep face up

rules: Cut out the mystery cards. Shuffle them and put them face down.
Lay the 9 sign cards face up where everyone can see them.
On your turn, take the top mystery card and read it out loud.
Choose a mat: ALIVE, NOT ALIVE or ARGUE IT. Put the card on it.
Give your reason. Point to at least one sign card that helped you decide. A good reason wins one token.
Anyone who disagrees can argue back with a different sign card. A good argument also wins a token.
When the cards run out, the player with the most tokens wins. Then look at the ARGUE IT mat together.

setup.art: Three paper mats on the floor labelled ALIVE, NOT ALIVE and ARGUE IT, with nine small sign cards in a row above them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three mats. Put the 9 sign cards above them.

setup.art: A child reading a mystery card about a candle flame aloud, holding it up.
setup.caption: 2. Take a mystery card and read it out loud.

setup.art: A child placing a card on the NOT ALIVE mat and pointing to the 'Made of cells' sign card.
setup.caption: 3. Put it on a mat and point to a sign card as your reason.

flow.do: 1. Lay the three mats on the floor. 2. Put the 9 sign cards in a row above them. 3. Shuffle the mystery cards face down. 4. Put the tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Every card is a puzzle. For each one, we decide: is it alive, not alive, or do scientists still argue about it? Then we give a reason, using these sign cards.
flow.kid: Lay out the three mats. Put the sign cards in a row. Mix the mystery cards. For each card, choose a mat. Then say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Alive, Not Alive, or Argue It! It is a card game about tricky cases. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Find the candle flame card. Play it together as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise. 'A candle flame. I eat wax, I need air, I grow and I make new flames.' Which signs does it have? Which sign cards does it not have?
flow.kid: Practice card: a candle flame. Which signs does it have? Which is it missing? Tap your answer.

ask.q: Which sign cards does the flame have?
good: It moves.
It takes in wax, like food.
It grows.
It makes waste like smoke.
It is not made of cells.
It does not pass on instructions.

check.q: A candle flame. Which mat does it go on?
options: ALIVE, because it eats, grows and makes new flames
NOT ALIVE, because it has no cells and no instructions
ARGUE IT, because scientists cannot decide
check.why: Fire passes many tests, but it has no cells, and a new flame carries no instructions from the old one. So scientists agree it is not alive. Picking ALIVE usually means counting the signs it has without checking the ones it lacks. Picking ARGUE IT is a fair guess, but fire is one case scientists do agree on.

flow.context: This is a practice round of Alive, Not Alive, or Argue It!, the tricky-cases card game.

flow.do: Take turns drawing cards. Each player places a card and gives a reason. Hand out a token for every good reason or good argument.
flow.say: Your turn. Read the card. Choose a mat. Point to a sign card and tell us why. If you disagree with someone, argue back with another sign card.
flow.kid: Take a card. Read it. Choose a mat. Point to a sign card and say why. You can argue back if you disagree.
flow.parent: Good reasons name a sign. For example: 'The seed is alive, because it is made of cells and it will grow when it gets water.' Expected places: virus, computer program and xenobot go well on ARGUE IT. The cloud, river, chair and robot go on NOT ALIVE (the chair is once-living). The seed, water bear, mule, mango, yeast, mushroom, curd bacteria, lotus seed and tree stump are ALIVE. The shop egg is a fine argument: it has never been sat on, so it will not grow a chick. Accept any well-argued answer.

ask.q: The mule can't have babies. Is it still alive?
good: Yes. It still eats, grows, breathes and is made of cells.
Making young is a sign for the kind of living thing, not for every single one.

flow.do: Pick up the water bear card and the dry seed card. Hold them up together.
flow.say: These two show almost no signs at all while they are dry. But we put them on ALIVE. Why?
flow.kid: The dry seed and the dry water bear do nothing. Why are they alive?

check.q: A dry water bear shows no signs of life. Why do scientists still say it is alive?
options: Because it is resting, and wakes up and lives again when water comes
Because all animals are alive, even dead ones
check.why: A dried water bear is dormant. Its life processes have nearly stopped, but its cells are not broken. Add water and it walks again. Picking 'all animals are alive' mixes up being an animal with being alive. A dead animal is not alive.

flow.context: This step of the tricky-cases card game looks at things that seem dead but are only resting.

flow.do: Count the tokens. Then look at the ARGUE IT mat together.
flow.say: Who has the most tokens? Now look at the ARGUE IT pile. These are the cards that even scientists argue about. Which one would you most like to find out about?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Look at the ARGUE IT pile. Which card is the biggest puzzle for you?
flow.think: If you had to make one new sign card that every living thing has, and nothing else has, what would it say?

games.title: The Sign Collectors
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or one child with the app
games.context: This is a collecting game. Each player is a tricky case, like fire or a robot. Players try to collect all nine signs of life. Nothing but a truly living thing can collect them all.

printables.title: 8 character cards (one per player, the rest kept as spares)
Sign sheet with 9 boxes for each player

rules: Each player takes one character card at random and reads it out.
Shuffle the sign cards and put them face down.
On your turn, draw a sign card and read it.
Ask: can my character honestly do this? If the others agree, tick that box on your sheet.
If not, put the card on the 'can't do it' pile and say why.
After 6 rounds each, everyone counts their ticks.
The winner is the character with the most ticks. Then everyone checks: did anyone tick 'Made of cells' and 'Passes on instructions'?

setup.art: A score sheet with nine empty boxes and a character card showing a candle flame beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Take a character card and a sign sheet.

setup.art: A child drawing a sign card that says 'Grows' from a face-down pile.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a sign card. Can your character really do it?

setup.art: A sign sheet with five ticks and four empty boxes, and the boxes 'Made of cells' and 'Passes on instructions' circled in red.
setup.caption: 3. Tick the signs you have. Check the last two boxes.

flow.do: 1. Deal one character card to each player. 2. Give each player a sign sheet. 3. Shuffle the sign cards face down.
flow.say: Each of you is now a tricky case. Your job is to collect signs of life. But you can only tick a sign if your character can honestly do it.
flow.kid: You are a tricky case now. Read your card. Collect signs of life. Only tick a sign your character can really do.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Sign Collectors, a game where each player is a tricky case like fire or a robot.

flow.do: Take turns. Draw a sign card, read it, and decide together whether the character can do it.
flow.say: Draw a sign. Can your character really do it? Tell us how. If the rest of us agree, tick it.
flow.kid: Draw a sign card. Can your character do it? Say how. If everyone agrees, tick it.
flow.parent: Expect fire to collect moving, energy, growing, waste and food, and maybe 'makes young' (sparks). Robots get moving and sensing. Crystals get growing. The mule gets everything except 'makes young'. The dry seed and the tun get 'made of cells' and 'passes on instructions', but little else while dry. The virus gets 'passes on instructions' and perhaps 'makes young', only inside a cell. Let the children argue it out.

check.q: The Candle flame player draws 'Made of cells'. Can they tick it?
options: Yes, because fire is hot like a body
No, because fire is a chemical change, not made of cells
check.why: Fire is fuel joining with oxygen. There are no cells in a flame. Picking 'grows' is a common trap: crystals and fires grow too, but growing alone does not make something alive.

flow.context: This is the main part of The Sign Collectors, the tricky-cases collecting game.

flow.do: Count the ticks. Compare the sheets side by side.
flow.say: Who has the most ticks? Now look at the last two boxes: made of cells, and passes on instructions. Who ticked them? Who didn't?
flow.kid: Count your ticks. Look at the last two boxes. Who ticked them?

ask.q: The fire got more ticks than the dry seed. So is fire more alive?
good: No. The seed has cells and instructions. Fire never does.
Counting signs is not enough. Some signs matter more.

flow.think: Which two signs are the hardest for a non-living thing to fake?

items.p: Scientists use many signs to decide if something is alive. Which of these is NOT enough on its own?
opts: Passing on instructions to its young
items.why: Moving alone tells us nothing. Rivers, clouds and cars move, and they are not alive. Being made of cells and passing on instructions are the two signs non-living things find hardest to fake.
items.art: A river, a cloud and a car all moving, with a question mark.

items.p: A candle flame moves, grows, uses wax and air, and gives off smoke. Why is it not alive?
opts: It has no cells, and a new flame carries no instructions from the old one
items.why: Fire does many things living things do. But it has no cells and passes on no instructions. Picking 'too hot' mixes up temperature with life. Some living things live in hot springs.

items.p: When the grown-up covered the candle with a glass, the flame went out. It had used up the ____ in the glass.
items.why: A flame needs oxygen, a gas in the air. So do we. Under the glass, the oxygen ran out.

items.p: Remember the sleeping seeds experiment, with seeds and pebbles on wet cotton? What happened to the pebbles?
items.why: The pebbles stayed the same, because they are not alive. Only the seeds grew. The pebbles show that water alone does not make things grow.

items.p: A dry moong seed in the kitchen jar does nothing for a year. What is it?
opts: Alive but resting, which is called dormant
items.why: A dry seed is dormant. Its life processes have slowed nearly to a stop. Give it water and warmth, and it wakes. Picking 'once-living' mixes it up with a dry leaf or wood, which can never grow again.

items.p: Alive but resting, with life almost stopped, is called ____.
items.why: Dormant means alive but resting. Seeds, dried yeast and dried water bears can all be dormant.

items.p: What is a water bear?
opts: A small brown bear that lives near water
A tiny eight-legged animal that lives in damp moss
items.why: A water bear, or tardigrade, is a tiny animal about half a millimetre long. It has eight stubby legs and lives in damp moss. Its name comes from the way it waddles like a bear.
items.art: A water bear on a strand of moss, drawn very big.

items.p: A dried-up water bear, curled into a tun, can wake up again when it gets water.
items.why: True. A tun is a water bear's resting form. When water comes back, it uncurls and walks again. Some have woken after about 30 years frozen.

items.p: How does a salt crystal grow?
opts: By adding more salt onto its outside
items.why: A crystal grows only by stacking more of the same particles onto its outside. Living things grow from inside, by turning food into new parts.

items.p: Where can a virus make copies of itself?
items.why: A virus can only make copies inside a living cell. On a table or in the air it does nothing at all. That is why scientists argue about whether it is alive.

items.p: Scientists all agree that viruses are alive.
items.why: False. Scientists still argue. Some say viruses are not alive, because they do nothing alone. Others say they are a kind of life, because they carry instructions, make copies and evolve.

items.p: A robot vacuum cleaner senses walls and moves by itself. What is it?
opts: Alive, because it senses and moves
Not alive, because it has no cells, does not grow and cannot make young
items.why: A robot follows instructions people wrote. It has no cells, does not take in food and cannot build a baby robot. Picking 'alive' means counting two signs and forgetting all the others.

items.p: Sort these into Alive, Not alive and Once alive.
items.why: The seed, yeast and mushroom are alive, even if resting. Fire, crystals and robots are not alive. Wood and cotton came from plants that were alive, so they are once alive.

items.p: Match each tricky case to the reason it is tricky.
pairs: It grows and makes new fires, but has no cells
It grows, but only by adding on outside
It does nothing, but it is alive
It makes copies, but only inside a cell
It moves and senses, but has no cells
items.why: Each tricky case passes some tests of life and fails others. That is what makes it tricky.

items.p: In the balloon test, only the bottles with yeast made gas. Write three sentences: what you think about dried yeast, what you saw, and why.
items.a: What I think: dried yeast is alive but resting. What I saw: the balloon on the warm yeast bottle grew, but the bottle without yeast made no gas. Why: the yeast woke up in warm sugar water, ate the sugar and gave off carbon dioxide.
items.why: This is claim, evidence and reasoning. Any answer with all three parts, using what was seen, is good.

items.p: Your friend says: 'Fire is alive, because it eats, breathes and grows.' What would you tell your friend?
items.a: Fire does do some of those things. But it has no cells, and a new fire gets no instructions from the old one. So scientists say it is not alive.
items.why: A good answer agrees with what is true in the friend's idea, then names the missing signs.

items.p: Fire and your cells both join fuel with oxygen. What is the big difference?
opts: Cells do it slowly, step by step, and under control. Fire does it wildly, all at once
items.why: Both give off energy, carbon dioxide and water. A cell does it so slowly and carefully that it stays warm but never burns. Picking 'no difference' forgets that cells have instructions controlling every step.

items.p: Lavoisier, a French scientist about 240 years ago, compared breathing to what?
items.why: Lavoisier showed that breathing is like a slow, gentle burning. His wife, Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, drew his experiments and wrote up his results.

items.p: A mule eats, grows and breathes, but almost never has babies. Is it alive?
opts: No, because living things must make young
Yes. It is made of cells and does all the other life processes
items.why: Making young is a sign for a kind of living thing, not for every single one. Mules, worker bees and many people never have young, and they are fully alive.

items.p: In the 1990s a NASA group suggested a working definition of life. What did it say?
opts: Life is a chemical system that keeps itself going and can evolve
Life is anything with a brain
items.why: The NASA working definition says life keeps itself going and can evolve over generations. It was written to help search for life on other planets. It is a tool, not a final answer.

items.p: A water bear's dry, curled-up resting form is called a ____.
items.why: A tun is a water bear with its legs pulled in and almost all its water gone. Its life nearly stops until water returns.

items.p: In 2007 scientists sent dried water bears into space, outside a spacecraft. What happened?
opts: Many survived, and later had babies
items.why: Many dried water bears survived the vacuum of space and some survived strong sunlight too. Back on Earth, they woke and later laid eggs. This shows how deeply they can rest.

items.p: Why do we get a new flu vaccine most years?
opts: Because the old vaccine goes bad
Because flu viruses change over time, so the vaccine must change too
Because vaccines are made of crystals
items.why: Flu viruses change a little every time they are copied. Over a year, they change enough that last year's vaccine may not match. This changing is evolution, one reason some scientists call viruses a kind of life.

items.p: Esther Lederberg discovered a virus that can hide inside bacteria for many generations.
items.why: True. In 1951 she discovered the virus lambda, which slips its instructions into a bacterium's own instructions and hides there. She got far less credit than her husband, who won a Nobel Prize.

items.p: Your hair grows every week, but cutting it does not hurt. Why?
opts: Hair is alive and very brave
The part of the hair you cut is made of dead cells. It is pushed out by living cells at the root
items.why: The hair you see is made of dead cells. Living cells under your skin, at the root, push it out. So hair 'grows' by being pushed from below, a little like a crystal growing from one side.

items.p: In 1668, Francesco Redi covered jars of meat with cloth. No maggots appeared. What did this show?
opts: Maggots come from eggs laid by flies, not from the meat itself
items.why: When flies could not reach the meat, no maggots came. So maggots come from flies' eggs. Living things only come from other living things.

items.p: Which of these is the best evidence that a dry seed is alive?
opts: Given water and warmth, it sends out a root, but a pebble never does
items.why: The comparison with the pebble is what makes the evidence strong. Both get water. Only the seed grows. That is why the sleeping seeds experiment uses a pebble plate.

items.p: Put the steps of a virus making copies in order.
items: The virus drifts until it touches a living cell
It gets its instructions inside the cell
The cell builds many new viruses
The new viruses burst out to find more cells
items.why: A virus does nothing until it reaches a cell. Then the cell does all the work of making copies.

items.p: Which signs of life does a candle flame show? Sort them.
cats: The flame does not show this
items: The flame does not show this
The flame does not show this
items.why: Fire shows many signs, but never cells or instructions. That is why it is not alive.

items.p: Why do we put a pebble plate next to the seeds in the sleeping seeds experiment? Write two sentences.
items.a: The pebbles get water too, so we can check that water alone does not make things grow. When the seeds grow and the pebbles don't, we know something inside the seed made the difference.
items.why: A comparison like this is called a control. It is what makes a test fair.

items.p: Write one way a dry seed and a dried water bear are the same, and one way they are different.
items.a: Same: both are alive but resting, and both wake up with water. Different: the seed is a plant and grows roots and leaves, but the water bear is an animal and walks.
items.why: Any true likeness and difference is good. Dormancy is the big likeness.

items.p: Most viruses are much smaller than bacteria. What do scientists need to see them?
opts: Nothing, they are easy to see
items.why: Most viruses are too small even for a school microscope. An electron microscope uses electrons instead of light, so it can show much smaller things.

items.p: In 2003, French scientists described the mimivirus. What was surprising about it?
opts: It was so big it was first mistaken for a bacterium
items.why: The mimivirus is a giant virus, with far more genes than other viruses. Later, scientists even found a smaller virus that attacks it. Giant viruses made the argument about whether viruses are alive even harder.

items.p: About 8 out of every 100 parts of your own instructions came from where?
opts: From viruses that hid inside our ancestors long ago
items.why: Long ago, some viruses hid their instructions inside our ancestors' cells, and the hidden pieces were copied down the generations. Some of these pieces now do useful jobs in our bodies.

items.p: Schrödinger said living things are special because they keep themselves in order using energy. Which non-living thing also does a little of this?
opts: A candle flame, which keeps its shape while wax and air flow through it
A salt crystal in a jar
items.why: A flame keeps its shape while new fuel and air flow through it all the time, a bit like a living thing. This is exactly why fire is such a tricky case. A stone does nothing to keep itself in order.

items.p: A lotus seed found in a dry lake bed in China was about 1,300 years old. What happened when scientists gave it water?
items.why: The seed had been dormant for about 1,300 years, and it still grew. Its cells had stayed alive, only resting, all that time.

items.p: In 1828, Friedrich Wöhler made urea, a chemical from living bodies, out of non-living chemicals. This helped show there is no special 'life force' in the chemicals of living things.
items.why: True. Wöhler's work helped show that the chemicals in living things are ordinary chemicals, made of ordinary atoms.

items.p: In 2020 scientists built 'xenobots' from frog cells. Why are they a puzzle?
opts: They are made of living cells, but they were designed by people, like machines
items.why: Xenobots are living cells arranged by people into a new shape. They move, and some even gathered loose cells into new xenobots. So are they living things or machines? They blur the line.

items.p: A rock from Mars, found in Antarctica, was once said to hold tiny fossils of Martian life. What do most scientists think now?
opts: Ordinary non-living chemistry could have made the shapes, so it is not good evidence
items.why: The tiny shapes in the rock, called ALH84001, could be made without life. Most scientists were not convinced. Big claims need strong evidence.

items.p: Which is the best reason the line between alive and not alive is fuzzy?
opts: Tricky cases like viruses and dormant seeds have some signs of life but not others, and every definition has a case that breaks it
items.why: Every definition so far has a tricky case. That does not mean anything goes. Fire, rocks and robots are clearly not alive, and trees clearly are. The fuzziness is at the edge.

items.p: J.C. Bose, a scientist in Kolkata, wrote a book in 1902 called 'Response in the Living and ____'.
items.why: Bose measured responses in plants and even in metals, and he felt there was no sharp break between living and non-living. Most scientists today agree with his plant measurements, but not with all his ideas.

items.p: Put the sleeping seed's waking-up in order.
items: The dry seed rests in the jar
It takes in water and swells
items.why: Water is the signal. The seed swells, its cells wake up and use stored food, then the root comes first and the shoot after.

items.p: Match each scientist to what they found.
pairs: A virus that hides inside bacteria
Gutter dust held tiny animals that woke in water
Breathing is like a slow burning
items.why: Each of these people moved the line between living and non-living, or showed where it really is.

items.p: Is a virus alive? Write what you think, and give one reason for and one reason against.
items.a: Any view is fine with good reasons. For: a virus carries instructions, makes copies and evolves. Against: it has no cells and can do nothing outside a living cell.
items.why: Scientists still argue about this. A strong answer gives both sides before choosing.

items.p: Design a test to find out whether something in a spoon of Mars soil is alive. Say how your test avoids being fooled by ordinary chemistry.
items.a: Add warm sugar water and cover with a balloon to catch any gas. Do the same with plain sand as a comparison. Then heat some soil strongly and test again. If gas only comes from the unheated soil, and not from the sand, something living may be there.
items.why: A good test has a comparison, like the pebble plate or the no-yeast bottle.

items.p: Some sages say the same life runs through everything. Most scientists say life is a special arrangement of ordinary atoms. Write what you think, and why.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer is good. For example: 'I think living things are made of the same atoms as everything else, so maybe we are not so separate. But only some things are arranged to be alive.'
items.why: This is an open question. There is no single right answer, only well-argued ones.

experiments.title: Sleeping Seeds: is a dry seed alive?
experiments.question: Is a dry seed alive, even though it does nothing? What does it need to wake up?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. What will happen to seeds on wet cotton? To pebbles on wet cotton? To seeds on dry cotton? Draw your guess for each plate.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, keep everything the same except one thing. Use the same plates, the same cotton and the same place. The wet seeds and the wet pebbles test whether water alone makes things grow. The wet seeds and the dry seeds test whether seeds need water. Use 6 seeds, because one seed can be a dud.

materials.item: dry whole moong seeds
small pebbles about the size of a moong seed
3 small steel plates or saucers
cotton wool or tissue
water in a cup
a ruler
a hand lens

experiments.safety: Do not eat raw seeds from the experiment. Wash hands after handling them. Keep pebbles away from very small children.

schedule.what: Guess what will happen. Set up the three plates. Draw them.
Check all three plates. Draw what you see. Add a few drops of water to plates 1 and 2.
Check, draw and measure the longest root. Water plates 1 and 2.
Check, draw and measure. Water plates 1 and 2.
Last check. Finish the table. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table each day. Draw the three plates side by side each day. On the last day, draw a line chart of the longest root on plate 1, one point for each day.
experiments.context: This is the sleeping seeds experiment. You put dry seeds and pebbles on wet cotton, and more dry seeds on dry cotton, and watch for five days.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: the longest moong root on wet cotton
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Three steel plates in a row, each with a layer of cotton: plate 1 wet with six moong seeds, plate 2 wet with six small pebbles, plate 3 dry with six moong seeds.
setup.caption: 1. Make three plates: wet seeds, wet pebbles, dry seeds.

setup.art: A child adding drops of water from a spoon onto the cotton of the first two plates.
setup.caption: 2. Keep plates 1 and 2 damp every day. Leave plate 3 dry.

setup.art: The first plate on day 4, with white roots curling out of the seeds and a ruler laid beside the longest root.
setup.caption: 3. Each day, draw all three plates and measure the longest root.

flow.do: Put a dry moong seed and a pebble side by side on your child's palm.
flow.say: Look at these two. Both are hard, both are still, both do nothing. One of them is alive. Which one, do you think? How could we test it?
flow.kid: Look at the seed and the pebble. Both do nothing. Which one is alive? How could you test it?

ask.q: How could we find out which one is alive?
good: Give them both water and see which one grows.
Watch them for a few days.

flow.context: This is the start of the sleeping seeds experiment. It asks whether a dry seed is alive, even though it does nothing.

flow.do: Help your child draw three plates and their guesses for each.
flow.say: Here is our plan. Plate 1: seeds on wet cotton. Plate 2: pebbles on wet cotton. Plate 3: seeds on dry cotton. What will happen on each plate? Draw your guess.
flow.kid: Draw three plates. Seeds on wet cotton. Pebbles on wet cotton. Seeds on dry cotton. Draw what you think will happen.

flow.do: 1. Put a layer of cotton on each plate. 2. Wet the cotton on plates 1 and 2 until damp but not swimming. 3. Leave plate 3 dry. 4. Put 6 seeds on plate 1, 6 pebbles on plate 2 and 6 seeds on plate 3. 5. Put the plates side by side, away from direct sun.
flow.say: We use two plates of seeds, so the only difference is the water. And we put pebbles on wet cotton, to check that water alone does not make things grow.
flow.kid: Put cotton on three plates. Wet plates 1 and 2. Keep plate 3 dry. Add seeds, pebbles and seeds. Put them side by side.
flow.parent: Cotton should be damp, like a squeezed sponge. Too much water can make seeds rot.

check.q: Why do we put pebbles on wet cotton too?
options: To check that water alone does not make things grow
check.why: The pebbles are a comparison. If pebbles stayed the same and the seeds grew, then something inside the seeds, not the water, made the difference. Picking 'pebbles are alive' is the very idea we are testing.

flow.do: Each day for four days, check all three plates. Draw them. Add a few drops of water to plates 1 and 2. Measure the longest root on plate 1.
flow.say: Let's check our plates. What has changed? Which plate looks different? Let's measure the longest root.
flow.kid: Check your plates. What has changed? Draw them. Measure the longest root.
flow.wait: Come back each day for four days.
flow.parent: Expect seeds on plate 1 to swell within a day. A white root appears on day 2 or 3, then a shoot. Pebbles and dry seeds stay the same. Use the hand lens to look at the root tip.

flow.do: On the last day, add water to plate 3, the dry seeds. Talk about what will happen next.
flow.say: Plate 3 has been dry all this time. Were those seeds dead, or still waiting? Let's give them water and see.
flow.kid: Plate 3 was dry all week. Are its seeds dead or waiting? Give them water. Check tomorrow.

check.q: The dry seeds did nothing all week. Then you gave them water, and next day they swelled up. What does this show?
options: They were dead and water brought them back to life
They were alive all along, resting until water came
check.why: The seeds were dormant: alive but resting. Their life processes went on very slowly all week. Picking 'dead and brought back' is how most people first explain it. But water can never bring dead things back to life. The pebbles show that.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Let's finish like scientists. What do you think now about dry seeds? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a dry seed is alive, only resting. What I saw: the seeds on wet cotton grew roots 40 mm long by day 5, but the pebbles on wet cotton did not change. Why: the seed has a baby plant inside that wakes up when it gets water.

experiments.title: The Balloon Test: is the sand in the yeast packet alive?
experiments.question: Dried yeast looks like sand. Is it alive?
experiments.predict: Guess which bottle will blow up its balloon: yeast with warm sugar water, yeast with cold sugar water, or warm sugar water with no yeast.
experiments.fair_test: Keep everything the same except one thing at a time. Each bottle gets the same amount of water and sugar. Bottles 1 and 2 test whether warmth matters. Bottles 1 and 3 test whether the yeast is what makes the gas.
results_table: Distance round the balloon after 30 minutes (cm)

materials.item: dried yeast (1 packet)
sugar
3 small empty plastic bottles of the same size
3 balloons
warm water (bath-warm) and cold water from the fridge
a funnel or a rolled paper cone
a piece of string and a ruler

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the warm water. It must feel like bath water, not hot. Do not drink the mixture.

schedule.what: Set up three bottles. Watch the balloons for 30 minutes. Measure them. Explain what happened.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the three bottles and their balloons after 30 minutes.
experiments.context: This is the balloon test. You put dried yeast in sugar water in a bottle, with a balloon on top, to see if the yeast does anything a living thing does.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: distance round each balloon after 30 minutes
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Three small plastic bottles in a row labelled 1, 2 and 3, with a spoon of sugar going into each.
setup.caption: 1. Put 1 teaspoon of sugar in each bottle.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring warm water into bottles 1 and 3 and cold water into bottle 2, and a child tipping yeast through a paper cone into bottles 1 and 2.
setup.caption: 2. Add water. Add yeast to bottles 1 and 2 only.

setup.art: Three bottles with balloons stretched over their necks, the balloon on bottle 1 standing up and half full.
setup.caption: 3. Stretch a balloon over each neck. Watch for 30 minutes.

flow.do: Pour a little dried yeast into your child's palm. Let them look at it with the hand lens.
flow.say: This is dried yeast, from the kitchen shop. It looks like sand. Bakers say it is alive. What do you think? How could we test it?
flow.kid: Look at the dried yeast with the lens. It looks like sand. Is it alive? How could you find out?
flow.context: This is the start of the balloon test. It asks whether dried yeast, which looks like sand, is alive.

flow.do: 1. Put 1 teaspoon of sugar in each bottle. 2. A grown-up pours half a cup of warm water into bottles 1 and 3, and half a cup of cold water into bottle 2. 3. Add 1 teaspoon of yeast to bottles 1 and 2 only. 4. Swirl each bottle. 5. Stretch a balloon over each neck.
flow.say: Bottle 1 has yeast and warm water. Bottle 2 has yeast and cold water. Bottle 3 has warm water and no yeast. Which balloon do you think will blow up?
flow.kid: Put sugar in all three bottles. A grown-up adds water. Add yeast to bottles 1 and 2. Swirl. Put on the balloons.
flow.parent: Warm means bath-warm, about as warm as your wrist can comfortably hold. Water that is too hot can kill the yeast.

flow.do: Watch the bottles for 30 minutes. Check at 10 minutes and at 30 minutes. Look for bubbles and froth.
flow.say: Let's look at the bottles. Do you see bubbles? Froth? Is any balloon standing up? Living things take in food and give off waste. What could the gas be?
flow.kid: Look at the bottles. Do you see bubbles? Is a balloon filling up? Check again in a while.
flow.parent: Bottle 1 should froth and its balloon should slowly stand up and fill. Bottle 2 will be slow. Bottle 3 will not change. The gas is carbon dioxide, the same gas you breathe out.

flow.do: Wrap a string around the middle of each balloon. Measure the string against the ruler.
flow.say: Let's measure how big each balloon got. Wrap the string around its fattest part, then hold it on the ruler.
flow.kid: Wrap the string round each balloon. Measure the string with the ruler. Write it down.

check.q: Only the yeast bottles made gas. What does this tell us about dried yeast?
options: It is alive: it was resting, and in warm sugar water it ate sugar and gave off gas
check.why: Yeast is a tiny fungus. Dried yeast is dormant. In warm sugar water it wakes, eats sugar and breathes out carbon dioxide gas, which fills the balloon. Bottle 3 had sugar and no yeast, and made no gas. So 'sugar makes gas by itself' does not fit the evidence.

flow.do: Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Let's finish like scientists. What do you think now about the yeast? What did you see? And why do you think it happened? Why was bottle 2 so slow?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why. Why was the cold bottle slow?
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: dried yeast is alive but resting. What I saw: the warm yeast balloon grew to 30 cm round, but the no-yeast balloon stayed at 10 cm. Why: the yeast woke up, ate the sugar and gave off gas. Cold slows living things down.

experiments.title: The Crystal Garden: it grows, but is it alive?
experiments.question: Salt crystals grow. Does that make them alive?
experiments.predict: Guess what will happen to a thread hanging in very salty water. Will anything grow? If it does, will it be alive?
experiments.fair_test: Set up a second jar with plain water and a thread, as a comparison. Keep both jars in the same quiet place, so only the salt is different.
results_table: Salty jar: what you see on the thread
Plain water jar: what you see

materials.item: salt
2 clean glass jars
hot water from the tap or kettle (a grown-up pours)
cotton thread and 2 pencils
a hand lens
a ruler

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours and stirs the hot water. Let the jars cool before your child touches them.

schedule.what: Make the salty water and the plain water. Hang the threads. Guess what will happen.
Look at both threads with the hand lens. Draw them.
Look again. Measure the biggest crystal. Draw.
Last look. Compare with the sleeping seeds. Put the crystal on trial with the signs of life.

experiments.record: Draw the thread each time you look. Write the size of the biggest crystal.
experiments.context: This is the crystal garden. You hang a thread in very salty water, and salt crystals slowly grow on it. Then you ask if growing makes something alive.

setup.art: A grown-up stirring salt into a jar of hot water, spoon by spoon, until some salt stays at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up stirs salt into hot water until no more dissolves.

setup.art: A cotton thread tied to a pencil laid across the top of the jar, the thread hanging into the salty water.
setup.caption: 2. Hang a thread from a pencil into the jar. Do the same with plain water.

setup.art: The thread a week later, covered with small white cube-shaped crystals, seen through a hand lens.
setup.caption: 3. Leave the jars still. Look at the threads every two days.

flow.do: Show your child some salt grains through the hand lens.
flow.say: Look at these salt grains. What shape are they? These are crystals. We are going to grow bigger ones. If they grow, are they alive?
flow.kid: Look at salt grains with the lens. What shape are they? We will grow bigger ones. If they grow, are they alive?
flow.context: This is the start of the crystal garden. It asks whether something that grows has to be alive.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pours hot water into a jar. 2. Stir in salt, one spoon at a time, until a little stays at the bottom. 3. Fill the second jar with plain hot water. 4. Tie a thread to each pencil. 5. Lay a pencil across each jar so the thread hangs in the water. 6. Put both jars somewhere still.
flow.say: The hot water can hold lots of salt. As it cools and slowly dries up, the salt has to come out again. Let's see where it goes.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes the salty water. Hang a thread in it. Hang another thread in plain water. Leave both jars very still.

flow.do: On days 3, 5 and 7, look at both threads with the hand lens. Draw them. Measure the biggest crystal.
flow.say: What is on the threads? How are the crystals growing? From inside, or by adding on at the outside?
flow.kid: Look at both threads with the lens. What do you see? Draw it. Measure the biggest crystal.
flow.parent: Crystals usually appear in 2 to 4 days and keep growing as the water dries up. The plain water thread stays bare. Notice the flat faces and square corners of salt crystals.

flow.do: Put the crystal thread next to the moong seedlings from the sleeping seeds experiment, if you did it. Go through the signs of life one by one.
flow.say: Let's put our crystal on trial. Does it move? Eat? Get energy from food? Sense? Make young? Get rid of waste? Is it made of cells? Now the seedling. What is the difference in how they grew?
flow.kid: Put your crystal on trial. Go through each sign. Then try the seedling. How did each one grow?

check.q: The crystal and the seedling both grew. What is the big difference?
options: The crystal grew by adding salt on the outside. The seedling grew from inside, by turning water and air into new parts
There is no difference, so both are alive
check.why: A crystal grows only by stacking more of the same particles on its outside. A seedling takes in water and air and builds new parts, like a root and leaves, from inside its cells. Picking 'no difference' usually means treating any growing as a sign of life. Growing alone is not enough.

flow.do: Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: What do you think now: is the crystal alive? What did you see? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: the crystal is not alive. What I saw: it grew to 5 mm, but only salt built up on the outside, and it did nothing else. The plain water thread stayed bare. Why: the salt came out of the water as it dried. The crystal has no cells and takes in no food.

activities.title: The Mystery Tray

materials.item: a tray or a big plate
a pebble, a dry moong seed, a candle (not lit), a fresh leaf, a dry leaf, a spoon of salt, a toy car, a cotton thread, a feather and a slice of bread
3 sheets of paper labelled ALIVE, NOT ALIVE and ONCE ALIVE

activities.safety: Nothing on the tray is eaten. Watch small children with pebbles and seeds.

schedule.what: Look closely at ten things. Sort them into alive, not alive and once alive. Mark the ones you are not sure about.

activities.record: Take a photo of the sorted tray, or draw it. Put a question mark on every thing you were not sure about.
activities.context: This is a noticing activity. Your child looks closely at ten everyday things on a tray and sorts them into alive, not alive and once alive, before learning anything.

setup.art: A steel tray holding a pebble, a dry moong seed, an unlit candle, a green leaf, a brown dry leaf, a little heap of salt, a toy car, a cotton thread, a feather and a slice of bread.
setup.caption: 1. Put ten everyday things on a tray.

setup.art: A child looking at a dry seed through a hand lens, with three paper labels on the floor: ALIVE, NOT ALIVE and ONCE ALIVE.
setup.caption: 2. Look closely. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

setup.art: The ten things sorted onto the three labels, with small paper question marks on the seed, the candle and the bread.
setup.caption: 3. Sort them. Put a question mark on the hard ones.

flow.do: Put the tray in front of your child. Do not explain anything yet.
flow.say: Here are ten things from our home. Look very closely at each one. What do you notice? What do you wonder about?
flow.kid: Look closely at each thing on the tray. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

good: The seed looks like a tiny pebble.
The leaf is still green.
The bread has holes in it.

flow.context: This is the start of the Mystery Tray. Your child looks at ten everyday things before sorting them.

flow.do: Lay the three labels on the floor. Your child sorts each thing onto one label.
flow.say: Put each thing on a label: alive, not alive, or once alive. Once alive means it was part of a living thing, but is not alive now. Put a question mark on any you are not sure about.
flow.kid: Sort each thing. Alive, not alive, or once alive. Once alive means it used to be part of something living. Mark the hard ones with a question mark.
flow.parent: Do not correct anything yet. Most children put the seed with the pebble, and many put the candle near 'alive' because it can burn. Both are perfect puzzles for this unit. Bread is made from wheat, which was alive, and it holds yeast that was alive.

flow.do: Pick up the seed and the pebble. Then the candle.
flow.say: Which ones were hardest? Why? What would you need to see to be sure the seed is alive? What would you need to see to be sure the candle is not?
flow.kid: Which ones were hard? What test could prove the seed is alive?

check.q: Which thing on the tray is alive right now, even though it does nothing?
check.why: The dry seed is alive but resting. Give it water and it grows a root. A pebble never can. Picking the toy car usually means 'it can move, so it might be alive'. But moving alone tells us nothing.

flow.think: Keep your tray. At the end of this unit, sort it again. Will you change anything?

activities.title: Put the Candle on Trial

materials.item: a small candle on a steel plate
a matchbox (grown-up only)
a clear glass tumbler
a cold steel spoon
a second, unlit candle
the sign cards from the game, or a list of the signs of life

activities.safety: A grown-up lights and handles the candle the whole time. Tie back long hair. Keep paper away. Put the flame out at the end and let the tumbler cool before touching.

schedule.what: Test the candle flame against each sign of life. Decide: alive or not?

activities.record: Draw a two-column chart: 'Signs the flame showed' and 'Signs it lacked'. Write your verdict at the bottom.
activities.context: This is a trial. A grown-up lights a candle, and together you test the flame against each sign of life to decide if fire is alive.

setup.art: A grown-up lighting a small candle on a steel plate, with a glass tumbler and a steel spoon beside it.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up lights a candle on a steel plate.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a cold steel spoon just above the flame, with a black smudge of soot and a little mist on the spoon.
setup.caption: 2. Hold a cold spoon high above the flame. Look for mist and soot.

setup.art: A glass tumbler placed over the candle, the flame shrinking to a tiny blue dot.
setup.caption: 3. Cover the candle with a glass. Watch the flame.

flow.do: A grown-up lights the candle. Everyone sits back an arm's length away.
flow.say: Today the flame is on trial. We will test it, sign by sign. Does it move? Watch it. Does it grow? Watch the wick as the wax melts.
flow.kid: A grown-up lights the candle. Sit back. Watch the flame. Does it move? Does it change?
flow.context: This is the start of the candle trial. You test a candle flame against the signs of life.

flow.do: A grown-up holds a cold steel spoon about a hand's width above the flame for 3 seconds, then shows it.
flow.say: Look at the spoon. The mist is water, and the black smudge is soot. The flame makes waste, just like you do when you breathe out. Let's breathe on a cold spoon too.
flow.kid: Look at the spoon. There is mist and black soot. That is the flame's waste. Breathe on a cold spoon. What do you see?
flow.parent: Hold the spoon high enough that it never touches the flame. Wipe off the soot afterwards.

flow.do: A grown-up puts the glass tumbler gently over the candle. Watch until the flame goes out.
flow.say: Watch. The flame is using up something in the air. What happens when it runs out? We need that same thing, oxygen, to stay alive.
flow.kid: Watch the flame under the glass. What happens? It needed air, like you.

check.q: Why did the flame go out under the glass?
options: It used up the oxygen in the glass
check.why: A flame needs oxygen, a gas in the air. Under the glass it used the oxygen up, and could not get more. Picking 'finished its wax' is a fair guess, but the candle still has plenty of wax. The flame went out because the glass cut off the air.

flow.do: A grown-up lights the candle again. Then touches the wick of the second candle to the flame for a moment.
flow.say: Look. One flame has made a new flame. Is that like a cat having kittens? Does the new flame carry anything from the first one, the way kittens get instructions from their mother?
flow.kid: Watch. One flame lights another. Is that like a baby? Does the new flame get anything from the old one?

ask.q: Is the new flame like the old one's baby?
good: No. The new flame looks the way it does because of its own wax and wick, not because of the old flame.
Kittens get instructions from their mother. Flames get nothing.

flow.do: Blow out both candles. Fill in the two-column chart together.
flow.say: Let's sum up the trial. Which signs did the flame show? Which did it lack? Did it have cells? Did it pass on instructions? So, what is your verdict?
flow.kid: Fill in your chart. Signs the flame showed. Signs it lacked. Then give your verdict: alive or not alive?
flow.parent: A good verdict: 'Not alive. The flame moved, grew, used fuel and oxygen, made waste and started a new flame. But it has no cells and passes on no instructions.' If your child says it is a little bit alive, ask what it would need to be fully alive.

activities.title: Water Bear Hunt

materials.item: a small clump of dry moss from a wall, a tree trunk or a roof
a small bowl or a saucer of rainwater or bottled water
a clear plastic lid or a steel plate with a dark bottom
a dropper or a straw
a phone microscope clip, or a strong hand lens

activities.safety: A grown-up goes with you to collect moss. Take only a thumb-sized clump. Wash hands afterwards. Never touch your eyes while handling moss.

schedule.what: Collect a small clump of dry moss. Put it in a bowl of water overnight.
Squeeze the moss water onto a dark plate. Search for tiny eight-legged animals with a lens or a phone microscope.

activities.record: Draw everything that moves. If you find a water bear, count its legs and draw how it walks.
activities.context: This is a hunt for water bears, the tiny eight-legged animals that can dry out and wake up again. You soak dry moss in water and search the water for them.

setup.art: A grown-up and a child gently pulling a thumb-sized clump of dry moss from an old brick wall.
setup.caption: 1. With a grown-up, collect a small clump of dry moss.

setup.art: The clump of moss soaking in a small bowl of water on a windowsill overnight.
setup.caption: 2. Soak it in water overnight. The water bears wake up.

setup.art: A phone with a clip-on microscope lens held over a dark plate with drops of moss water, and on the screen a chubby eight-legged water bear.
setup.caption: 3. Squeeze the moss onto a dark plate. Search with a lens.

flow.do: With your child, find a wall, tree or roof with moss on it. Take one thumb-sized clump. At home, put it in a bowl of water overnight.
flow.say: This moss is dry, and so are any water bears living in it. They have curled into tiny dry balls called tuns. If we give them water tonight, they may wake up by tomorrow.
flow.kid: Find some dry moss with a grown-up. Take a small clump. Put it in water overnight. Any water bears in it may wake up.
flow.context: This is the start of the water bear hunt. You collect dry moss and soak it.

flow.do: Next day, squeeze the moss over the dark plate. Use the dropper to spread the water in small drops. Search each drop slowly with the phone microscope or lens.
flow.say: Water bears are about as long as a grain of salt is wide. Look for a slow, chubby animal that waddles on eight stumpy legs. Be patient. Many hunters look for a long time.
flow.kid: Squeeze the moss onto the plate. Look at each drop slowly. Look for a chubby animal with eight short legs.
flow.parent: Water bears are common but tiny, about half a millimetre long. With a hand lens you may only see a slowly moving speck. A phone microscope clip of 30 times or more helps a lot. You will probably also see other tiny moss animals, like wriggling rotifers. They can dry out and wake again too. If you find nothing, that is normal. Try moss from another place.

flow.do: Talk about what you found, even if it was not a water bear.
flow.say: Yesterday this moss was dry and nothing in it moved. Today there may be tiny animals swimming. Were they dead yesterday? Or waiting?
flow.kid: Did anything move in the water? Yesterday the moss was dry. Were those animals dead, or waiting?

check.q: Tiny animals swim in the water from dry moss. Where did they come from?
options: The water made them out of nothing
They were in the dry moss all along, resting, and woke up in the water
They hatched from the moss leaves
check.why: They were in the moss all along, dried out and resting. Water woke them. Picking 'the water made them' is the old idea of spontaneous generation. Scientists showed long ago that living things only come from other living things.

activities.title: Act It Out: A Day in the Life of a Virus

materials.item: a cardboard box with a door cut in one side (the cell)
about 20 building blocks or folded paper squares (the cell's building parts)
a folded paper with 'Make more of me' written on it (the virus's instructions)
a paper cap or a bowl as the virus coat

activities.safety: Clear a space so nobody trips.

schedule.what: Act out a virus outside a cell and inside a cell. Talk about whether it is alive.

activities.record: Draw a comic in three boxes: the virus drifting, the virus getting in, and the cell making copies.
activities.context: This is a drama game. One person plays a virus and one plays a living cell, to show how a virus can only make copies inside a cell.

setup.art: A cardboard box with a small door, labelled CELL, full of building blocks, and a child holding a folded paper labelled MAKE MORE OF ME.
setup.caption: 1. The box is the cell. The paper note is the virus's instructions.

setup.art: A child in a paper cap standing very still in the middle of a room, labelled VIRUS OUTSIDE A CELL.
setup.caption: 2. The virus stands still. Alone, it can do nothing.

setup.art: A parent inside the 'cell' reading the note and quickly building many small paper copies of the virus.
setup.caption: 3. Inside the cell, the cell reads the note and builds copies.

flow.do: Your child wears the paper cap and holds the note. Ask them to try to do the signs of life alone: eat, grow, move by themselves.
flow.say: You are a virus now. You are just a note of instructions in a coat. Outside a cell, a virus cannot eat, grow, or move by itself. So stand perfectly still. The wind carries you.
flow.kid: You are a virus. You are only a note in a coat. Alone, you can't eat or grow. Stand still. The wind carries you.
flow.context: This is the start of the virus drama. Your child plays a virus floating outside a cell.

flow.do: The parent is the cell, sitting by the box full of blocks. Your child drifts to the box and pushes the note through the door.
flow.say: Now you bump into a living cell. You slip your instructions inside. The cell reads them, without knowing what they are.
flow.kid: You drift to the cell. Push your note through the door. The cell reads it.
flow.parent: Read the note aloud in a robot voice: 'Make more of me.'

flow.do: The parent uses the blocks to build as many small 'virus' shapes as possible in one minute, then pushes them out of the door.
flow.say: Look. The cell is using its own building parts and its own energy to make copies of you. You did not do any of the work. Now the new viruses burst out to find more cells.
flow.kid: Watch the cell build copies of you. It does all the work. Now the copies burst out.

good: The cell did.
The cell used its own parts and energy.

flow.do: Sit down together and talk.
flow.say: So, is a virus alive? It cannot do anything alone. But it makes copies of itself, and it changes over time. Scientists still argue. What do you think?
flow.kid: Is a virus alive? It can't do anything alone. But it makes copies. What do you think? Why?

check.q: Why do scientists argue about whether viruses are alive?
options: Because viruses are too big to see
Because a virus makes copies of itself, but only inside a living cell, and does no life processes alone
Because viruses are made of metal
check.why: A virus carries instructions and makes copies, like living things. But it can only do this inside a cell, and alone it does nothing. That is why it sits on the edge. Picking 'animals' is a common mix-up. Viruses have no cells at all, while every animal is made of many cells.

activities.title: Is My Toy Robot Alive?

materials.item: a battery toy that moves or makes sounds, or a phone
a pet, a houseplant or a potted tulsi plant to compare
paper and pencil

activities.safety: Do not open battery boxes. Be gentle with pets.

schedule.what: Test a toy against the signs of life. Compare it with a living thing. Design what it would need to be alive.

activities.record: Make a table with two columns, the toy and the living thing, and a tick or cross for each sign.
activities.context: This activity puts a moving toy or a phone on trial against the signs of life, and compares it with a pet or a plant.

setup.art: A battery toy car and a potted tulsi plant side by side on a table, with a blank two-column table on paper.
setup.caption: 1. Put a moving toy next to a living thing.

setup.art: A child ticking boxes on the table with a pencil while the toy car moves.
setup.caption: 2. Test each sign of life for both.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a robot with extra parts labelled 'grows', 'finds its own food' and 'makes baby robots'.
setup.caption: 3. Draw what the toy would need to be alive.

flow.do: Switch the toy on. Go through each sign of life for the toy, then for the plant or pet.
flow.say: Does the toy move? Sense? Grow? Eat? Get rid of waste? Make young? Is it made of cells? Now let's try the tulsi plant.
flow.kid: Switch on the toy. Does it move, sense, grow, eat or make babies? Now test the plant.
flow.context: This is the start of the robot trial. You test a moving toy against the signs of life.

flow.do: Look at the table together.
flow.say: The toy moves and maybe senses. The plant hardly moves at all, but it ticks almost every box. So which is alive? What is the toy missing?
flow.kid: Look at your table. Which has more ticks? What is the toy missing?

check.q: A robot can sense walls and move by itself. Why is it still not alive?
options: Because it has no cells, does not grow or take in food, and cannot make young by itself
check.why: A robot follows instructions people wrote. It has no cells, does not grow, and cannot build a baby robot from food. Picking 'not green' mixes up being a plant with being alive. Animals are not green either, and they are alive.

flow.do: Your child draws a robot with all the extra parts it would need to be alive.
flow.say: Imagine you had to make this toy truly alive. What would you have to add? Draw it.
flow.kid: Draw the toy with everything it would need to be alive.
flow.think: If someone built a robot that could find its own food, repair itself and build copies, would you call it alive?

activities.title: Draw the Line

materials.item: a long piece of string or a dupatta, about 2 metres
two paper signs: SURELY ALIVE and SURELY NOT ALIVE
12 small paper cards: a stone, a crystal, fire, a robot, a cloud, a virus, a dry seed, a water bear in a tun, a bacterium, a mule, a tree and you

activities.safety: Lay the string flat so nobody trips.

schedule.what: Place cards along a line from surely alive to surely not alive. Talk about where the line should go.

activities.record: Take a photo of the line, or draw it. Mark where you would put the edge between alive and not alive.
activities.context: In this activity, the family lays a string across the floor, from 'surely alive' at one end to 'surely not alive' at the other, and places tricky cases along it.

setup.art: A long string across a floor, with a sign SURELY ALIVE at one end and SURELY NOT ALIVE at the other.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a string across the floor with a sign at each end.

setup.art: A family kneeling along the string, placing small cards: a tree near one end, a stone near the other, and a virus card in the middle.
setup.caption: 2. Everyone places the cards along the line.

setup.art: A child laying a ruler across the string at one point, marking 'the edge'.
setup.caption: 3. Decide: where does alive end? Mark the place.

flow.do: Lay the string out. Give each family member some cards. Take turns placing them along the string.
flow.say: Put each card somewhere along the string. The tree goes right at 'surely alive'. Where does the virus go? The dry seed? The fire?
flow.kid: Put each card along the string. Surely alive at one end. Surely not alive at the other. Where does each card go?
flow.context: This is the start of Draw the Line. Your family places tricky cases along a line from alive to not alive.

flow.do: Look at the cards in the middle. Each person moves one card they disagree with, and says why.
flow.say: Some cards ended up in the middle. Do you agree with where they are? Move one, and tell us why.
flow.kid: Look at the middle of the line. Move one card you disagree with. Say why.
flow.parent: There is no right line. Most families put the virus near the middle. The dry seed often starts near 'not alive' and moves towards 'alive' after the seed experiment. That movement is learning.

flow.do: Ask your child to put a ruler or a pencil across the string where they think 'alive' really begins.
flow.say: If you had to draw one sharp line, where would it go? Is it easy to choose? Why do you think scientists find it hard too?
flow.kid: Put a pencil across the string where 'alive' begins. Was that easy? Why or why not?

check.q: Why is it hard to draw one sharp line between alive and not alive?
options: Because some things, like viruses and dry seeds, have some signs of life but not others
check.why: Tricky cases sit in between. A virus makes copies but only inside a cell. A dry seed shows no signs, yet wakes later. Picking 'scientists have not tried' is not right. They have tried for hundreds of years, and the tricky cases are exactly what they argue about.

projects.title: The Museum of Tricky Cases

materials.item: a big sheet of chart paper or a tray for each exhibit
your crystal thread, sprouted seeds, a candle (unlit), a toy robot and drawings of a virus and a water bear
colour pencils and small paper label cards

projects.safety: Candles stay unlit in the museum.

schedule.what: Choose six tricky cases. Make a label card for each: signs it shows, signs it lacks, and a verdict.
Set up the museum. Give a tour to the family. Answer their questions.

projects.record: Keep the label cards. Take photos of the museum.
projects.context: In this project your child builds a small home museum of tricky cases, like fire, a crystal and a virus, with a label for each, and gives a tour.

setup.art: Six exhibits on a table: a crystal on a thread, a plate of moong sprouts, an unlit candle, a toy robot, a drawing of a virus and a drawing of a water bear, each with a folded label card.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out six tricky cases with a label card for each.

setup.art: A close-up label card with three parts: 'Signs I show', 'Signs I lack' and 'Verdict: alive, not alive or argued'.
setup.caption: 2. Fill in each label: signs it shows, signs it lacks, verdict.

setup.art: A child with a paper badge saying GUIDE, pointing at the virus drawing while parents listen.
setup.caption: 3. Give the family a tour and answer their questions.

flow.do: Help your child choose six cases and make a label card for each.
flow.say: A museum label tells visitors the most important things in a few words. For each case, write the signs it shows, the signs it lacks, and your verdict.
flow.kid: Choose six tricky cases. For each one, write: signs it shows, signs it lacks, and your verdict.
flow.wait: Finish the labels today. Set up the museum tomorrow.
flow.context: This is the first day of the Museum of Tricky Cases project. Your child makes a label for each exhibit.

flow.do: Set up the exhibits. Your child gives a tour. Each visitor asks one hard question.
flow.say: Welcome to the museum. Please tell us about each exhibit. Which one is the hardest to decide about?
flow.kid: Set up your museum. Give your family a tour. Answer one hard question about each exhibit.
flow.parent: Good hard questions: 'If the virus can make copies, why isn't it alive?' 'If the seed does nothing, how do you know it is alive?' 'Fire makes new fires. Isn't that having babies?'

check.q: A visitor says: 'The crystal grows, so it must be alive.' What is the best reply?
options: Crystals grow by adding on outside. They have no cells and take in no food, so growing alone does not make them alive
check.why: The crystal really does grow, so 'they do not really grow' is wrong. But it grows only by stacking more salt on the outside. Living things grow from inside, using food. 'Only animals grow' forgets plants, which grow all their lives.

challenges.title: Design a Life Detector for Mars
challenges.problem: A robot is going to Mars. It will dig up a spoon of soil. Your job is to design the tests it should do to find out whether anything in the soil is alive.
constraints: The robot can only test a tiny spoon of soil.
No human will be there to look.
The robot must not be fooled by fire, crystals or ordinary chemistry.
materials: a shoebox to build a model robot
a spoon of garden soil and a spoon of sand to practise on
general: Add water and food, and watch for gas, like the yeast balloon test.
Look through a microscope for cells.
Wait and see whether anything grows from inside or makes more of itself.
creative: Test the soil once, then heat it strongly and test again. If gas stops after heating, something living may have been killed. In 1976 NASA's Viking landers on Mars did tests like this. One test gave a puzzling result, and scientists still argue about what it meant.
Look for instructions, like the molecules inside cells that carry genes.
Test something you know is not alive, like sand, as a comparison. If the sand also 'passes', your test is fooled.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own test. Draw it, and say how it avoids being fooled by fire, crystals and chemistry.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You design the tests a robot on Mars should do to find out whether anything in a spoon of soil is alive.

setup.art: A model robot made from a shoebox with a spoon arm, scooping red soil on a pretend Mars surface.
setup.caption: 1. Picture the robot digging up a spoon of Mars soil.

setup.art: Two small cups, one of garden soil and one of sand, each with a little sugar water added and a balloon over the top.
setup.caption: 2. Practise your test on garden soil and on sand.

setup.art: A child's drawing of the robot with three labelled tests: 'add food, watch for gas', 'look for cells', 'heat, then test again'.
setup.caption: 3. Draw your robot's tests, step by step.

flow.do: Read the problem together. List the signs of life your child knows.
flow.say: Our robot is alone on Mars. Which signs of life can it test in a spoon of soil? Which ones are hard to test?
flow.kid: Your robot is alone on Mars. Which signs of life can it test in a spoon of soil?
flow.context: This is the start of the Mars life detector challenge.

flow.do: Practise one test at home. Put a spoon of garden soil in one cup and a spoon of sand in another. Add a teaspoon of sugar water to each and stretch a balloon over each cup. Check after 2 hours.
flow.say: Garden soil is full of tiny living things. Sand from a packet has very few. If our test works, which cup should make more gas?
flow.kid: Add sugar water to soil and to sand. Cover both with a balloon. Check later. Which one made gas?
flow.parent: The soil balloon may only crinkle a little. Bacteria in soil give off a small amount of carbon dioxide. Look for tiny bubbles in the soil too.

flow.do: Your child draws the robot and its tests, with a way to avoid being fooled.
flow.say: How will your robot be sure it found life, and not just a chemical fizz? Draw your plan.
flow.kid: Draw your robot and its tests. How will it avoid being fooled?

check.q: Why test plain sand next to the Mars soil?
options: As a comparison: if the sand passes the test too, the test is fooled by ordinary chemistry
check.why: A comparison shows what happens without life. If sand fizzes as much as the Mars soil, the fizz is chemistry, not life. This is exactly the pebble plate in the sleeping seeds experiment. Picking 'sand is alive' is the opposite of the idea.

challenges.title: Keep a Seed Asleep for a Year
challenges.problem: A farmer wants to save her best seeds for next year's sowing. Design a way to keep them asleep, so they do not sprout or rot, but still wake up next year.
constraints: Use only things found at home.
The seeds must still sprout after storage.
No chemicals that could harm people or animals.
general: Dry the seeds well in the sun first, because water wakes them up.
Store them in an airtight jar, so damp air cannot get in.
Keep the jar somewhere cool and dark.
creative: Many Indian farmers store grain with dried neem leaves to keep insects away.

Seed banks freeze dried seeds far below zero. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway, opened in 2008, keeps seeds from almost every country in a frozen mountain. In India, a national gene bank in New Delhi also keeps seeds cold.
Test your method. Store some seeds now. Sprout a few each month, and count how many wake up.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own seed-sleep box. Draw it, store some seeds, and plan when you will test them.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You design a way to keep seeds dormant, alive but asleep, for a whole year, the way seed banks do.

setup.art: Moong seeds spread on a steel plate drying in the sun on a balcony.
setup.caption: 1. Dry the seeds in the sun for a day.

setup.art: Dry seeds being poured into a small glass jar with a few dried neem leaves, and the lid being screwed on tight.
setup.caption: 2. Put them in an airtight jar. Add dry neem leaves if you like.

setup.art: A labelled jar on a shelf in a cool cupboard, with a calendar beside it marked 'test a few each month'.
setup.caption: 3. Keep the jar cool and dark. Test a few seeds each month.

flow.do: Talk about what wakes a seed up, from the sleeping seeds experiment.
flow.say: Remember the seeds on wet cotton? What woke them up? So, to keep a seed asleep, what must we keep away from it?
flow.kid: What woke the seeds on the wet cotton? So what must you keep away to keep a seed asleep?

good: Water.
Warmth.
Air too.

flow.context: This is the start of the seed-sleep challenge. You use what you learned about dormant seeds.

flow.do: Your child dries some seeds, puts them in a jar and designs the storage place.
flow.say: Let's make your seed-sleep box. Dry the seeds, seal the jar, and choose a cool, dark place. Write the date on the label.
flow.kid: Dry the seeds. Put them in a jar. Close it tight. Choose a cool, dark place. Write today's date on it.

check.q: Why must the seeds be very dry before you store them?
options: Water wakes seeds up, so damp seeds may sprout or rot in the jar
check.why: Water is the main signal that tells a dormant seed to wake. In a closed jar, a damp seed may start to sprout, then rot. Picking 'taste better' misses the point. We are keeping the seed alive, not cooking it.

flow.do: Plan the test: sprout 6 seeds from the jar each month on wet cotton.
flow.say: How will we know if your method works? Each month we will sprout 6 seeds. If most still wake up, your seed-sleep box works.
flow.kid: Each month, sprout 6 seeds from your jar. Count how many wake up.
flow.think: Seed banks keep seeds for many years. Why might it matter to keep old kinds of seeds alive?

videos.title: What Is Life? Is Death Real?
videos.why: For the parent and curious older children. A beautifully animated look at why life is hard to define, with viruses and other edge cases.
videos.check: Video id not known for sure. Search the channel for this title, check it is the Kurzgesagt video about defining life, and watch it first. Some parts go beyond Class 3.

videos.title: A video showing living tardigrades (water bears) under a microscope
videos.channel: Journey to the Microcosmos, or a similar microscope channel
videos.why: So children can see real water bears walking, before or after the water bear hunt.
videos.check: Video id not known for sure. Find a video with real microscope footage of living tardigrades. Check it shows real animals, not only animation, and that any claims about surviving heat or space match this unit.

videos.title: A short children's video on how viruses make copies inside cells
videos.channel: SciShow Kids, or another trusted science channel for children
videos.why: To show, with animation, what the virus drama game acts out: a virus getting into a cell and the cell making copies.
videos.check: Video id not known for sure. Find and watch first. Make sure it says viruses need a living cell to make copies, and does not frighten young children.

quiz.p: Which sign alone tells us that something is alive?
opts: None of them alone. We need to look at many signs together
quiz.why: No single sign is enough. Fire moves and grows. Crystals grow. A dry seed does neither, yet is alive. Picking 'moving' or 'growing' is the most common trap.

opts: It has no cells, and passes on no instructions
quiz.why: Fire moves, grows, uses fuel and air, and makes waste. But it has no cells and passes on no instructions.

quiz.p: How is a growing crystal different from a growing seedling?
opts: The crystal adds on outside. The seedling grows from inside using food
The seedling is made of salt
quiz.why: A crystal stacks more particles on its outside. A seedling builds new parts from inside its cells. Picking 'no difference' treats any growing as a sign of life.

opts: A seed that is alive but resting
A seed that has already grown
quiz.why: Dormant means alive but resting. Picking 'dead' is the most common first answer. But a dead seed never wakes, and a dormant one does.

quiz.p: What does a dried-up water bear need to wake up?
quiz.why: Water wakes a tun. The water bear soaks it up, uncurls and walks again.

quiz.p: In the sleeping seeds experiment, seeds and pebbles both sat on wet cotton. Only the seeds grew. What does this show?
opts: Something inside the seed, not just the water, made it grow
quiz.why: The pebbles are the comparison. They got the same water and did not change. So the seed's own life made the difference. Picking 'water makes anything grow' ignores the pebble plate.

quiz.p: What does a virus need to make copies of itself?
quiz.why: A virus can only make copies inside a living cell, using the cell's parts and energy. Alone, it does nothing.

quiz.p: Do all scientists agree about whether viruses are alive?
quiz.why: Scientists still disagree. Viruses make copies and evolve, but do nothing outside a cell. Both 'yes' answers pretend the question is settled.

quiz.p: A robot senses a wall and turns away. Why is it still not alive?
opts: It has no cells, does not grow or take in food, and cannot make young
quiz.why: A robot follows instructions people wrote. Sensing and moving are only two of the signs. Picking 'not green' confuses being a plant with being alive.

quiz.p: In the balloon test, why did one bottle have warm sugar water but no yeast?
opts: To make it fair, as a comparison, to show sugar water alone makes no gas
Because we ran out of yeast
quiz.why: The no-yeast bottle is the comparison. It shows that the gas came from the yeast, not from the sugar water.

quiz.p: Who decides exactly where the line between alive and not alive goes?
opts: Nature has one sharp line that everyone can see
People do, with definitions, and they still argue about the edge
quiz.why: Nature gives us real differences, like cells and instructions. But the exact edge, where viruses and dormant things sit, is drawn by people, and scientists still argue about it.

quiz.p: Do scientists know exactly how the first living thing began?
opts: No. They have ideas and experiments, but nobody knows for sure
It came from a crystal, everyone agrees
quiz.why: Nobody knows yet. Miller and Urey made some building blocks of life from gases in 1952, and there are ideas like the RNA idea, but the question is still open.

applications: Farmers and seed banks store seeds dry and cool, so they stay dormant and alive for years.
Bakers use dried yeast that wakes up in warm water and makes bread dough rise.
Doctors and scientists make vaccines by studying how viruses get into cells.
Scientists who study water bears hope to learn how to store medicines and vaccines dry, without a fridge.
NASA and ISRO design robots and tests to search for life on Mars and other worlds.
Food is kept in the fridge because cold slows down the bacteria and fungi that spoil it.
Dried fruits, papad and pickles last long because, without water, germs cannot grow well.
Fire fighters use the 'fire needs fuel, air and heat' idea. Take away one, and the fire dies.
Viruses that attack only bacteria, called phages, are being tested as medicines against infections.
Engineers build robots that copy living things, like walking, grasping or finding their way.
