spotted.art: A kitchen shelf with steel jars of rajma, chana and moong.

spotted.text: Moong sprouts at a sabzi stall: seeds that woke up.
spotted.art: A street stall with a bowl of fresh moong sprouts.

spotted.text: Green moss on an old wall after the monsoon. Water bears may be living in it.
spotted.art: A brick wall in a lane, covered in bright green moss.

spotted.text: A diya flame at a festival: moving, eating oil, breathing air, but not alive.
spotted.art: A clay diya with a bright flame on a doorstep.

spotted.text: Rock salt (sendha namak) at the grocer: a crystal that grew by adding on.
spotted.art: Pink chunks of rock salt in a shop bin.

spotted.text: A packet of dried yeast or a bakery's rising dough.
spotted.art: A ball of bread dough swelling in a bowl.

spotted.text: A sneeze: millions of cold viruses made by your own nose cells, flying out.
spotted.art: A child sneezing into a tissue, with tiny dots shown in a cloud.

spotted.text: A robot vacuum cleaner or a talking toy: moving and sensing, but not alive.
spotted.art: A round robot vacuum cleaner on a tiled floor.

open_questions.why_open: It depends on how you define life. Viruses do some things living things do but not others, and scientists have not agreed on a definition.

open_questions.q: How did the first living thing come from non-living chemicals?
open_questions.why_open: It happened about 4 billion years ago and left no clear traces. Experiments have made some building blocks, but no one has made life from scratch.

open_questions.q: Is a dried water bear alive while it is dry, or is it in a third state?
open_questions.why_open: Its life processes are so slow they are very hard to measure. Scientists argue about whether anything at all is happening inside.

open_questions.q: Is there life on other planets or moons, like Mars, Europa or Enceladus?
open_questions.why_open: We have only one example of life, on Earth. Missions are searching, but nothing has been found for sure yet.

open_questions.q: Could a machine or a computer program ever be alive?
open_questions.why_open: Some programs copy themselves and change, and some machines can repair themselves. Whether that counts as life depends on whether life must be made of cells and chemistry.

open_questions.q: How long can a seed stay dormant and still wake?
open_questions.why_open: Seeds of about 1,300 years old have grown. Nobody knows the true limit, and different seeds are very different.
Plants respond and send electrical signals, as J.C. Bose showed. But nobody knows whether there is any feeling behind it.

ask_kids: Is this cup of tea alive? Is the steam? Why not?
If you dried an ant, would it wake up in water like a water bear? Why not?
Which thing on this table do you think is the trickiest case?
The fan moves and the plant doesn't. Which one is alive?
Is a flame more alive than a seed? Why?
Are the sprouts in your lunch still alive?
When you have a cold, who is making all the viruses, you or the virus?
Is your shadow alive? It moves with you.
If a robot cried, would you think it was alive?
What is the most alive thing you saw today? The least alive?

jokes.j: Why did the seed refuse to get out of bed?
jokes.a: It was feeling dormant.

jokes.j: What did the candle say to the birthday cake?
jokes.a: I'm not alive, but I'm still the life of the party.

jokes.j: Why don't viruses ever get invited to parties?
jokes.a: They can't do anything on their own, and then they make copies of themselves everywhere.

jokes.j: What do you call a water bear who has been asleep for 30 years?
jokes.a: Well rested.

jokes.j: Why did the salt crystal not need a lunchbox?
jokes.a: It grows by stacking, not snacking.

jokes.j: What did the robot say to the tulsi plant?
jokes.a: You may not move, but you've got more ticks than me.

jokes.j: Why was the fire so hungry?
jokes.a: It was on a wax diet.

jokes.j: How do you wake up a sleeping seed?
jokes.a: Give it a gentle splash.

jokes.j: What is a water bear's favourite season?
jokes.a: The monsoon, of course. It finally gets to wake up.

jokes.j: Why did the yeast blow up the balloon?
jokes.a: It was a little gassy after all that sugar.

jokes.j: Why did the mule feel left out of the alive club?
jokes.a: Until someone said: you only need cells, not kids.

jokes.j: Knock knock. Who's there? Dormant. Dormant who?
jokes.a: Dormant wake me till it rains.

jokes.j: Why did the crystal go to school?
jokes.a: To grow on the outside and learn on the inside.

jokes.j: What did the virus say to the cell?
jokes.a: Can you make a few copies of this for me? Thousands, please.

jokes.j: Why was the tardigrade so calm in space?
jokes.a: It had already packed itself into a tun.

jokes.j: Why didn't the flame pass the life test?
jokes.a: It had no cells, just a hot temper.

jokes.j: What did the pebble say to the sprouting seed?
jokes.a: Show-off.

jokes.j: Why did the robot go to the doctor?
jokes.a: It had a virus. A computer one.

jokes.j: Which is the laziest living thing in the kitchen?
jokes.a: The rajma. It has been resting in that jar for months.

jokes.j: Why did the scientist put the seed on trial?
jokes.a: It was accused of only pretending to be dead.

jokes.j: What do you call a crystal that tells jokes?
jokes.a: A salty comedian.

jokes.j: Why did the cloud think it was alive?
jokes.a: It kept growing and having little clouds.

jokes.j: What did Maria say to the gutter dust?
jokes.a: Don't play dead with me.

jokes.j: Why are seed banks so rich?
jokes.a: Because everything they keep keeps growing in value.

maths.problem: In the sleeping seeds experiment, 6 moong seeds went on wet cotton. By day 5, 5 of them had grown a root. What fraction of the seeds woke up?
maths.answer: 5 out of 6, which is five sixths.
maths.explain: There were 6 seeds in all. 5 of them grew a root. So 5 out of 6 woke up. We write this as the fraction five sixths. Only 1 seed out of 6 did not wake. That one may have died, or may need more time.
maths.context: This is about the sleeping seeds experiment, where you put 6 dry moong seeds on wet cotton and watched which ones grew a root.
maths.why_maths: Seed banks test stored seeds this way. A fraction tells them how many of their seeds are still alive.

maths.problem: Look at the chart of the longest moong root. On day 3 it was 12 mm long. On day 5 it was 40 mm long. How much did it grow in those two days?
maths.explain: On day 5 the root was 40 mm. On day 3 it was 12 mm. 40 take away 12 is 28. So the root grew 28 mm in two days. That is about 14 mm each day.

chart.title: The longest moong root on wet cotton (made-up example)

maths.context: This is about the sleeping seeds experiment. You measured the longest root on the wet cotton plate every day.
maths.why_maths: Taking one measurement from another shows how fast something grew. Fast growth from inside is a sign of a living thing waking up.

maths.problem: In the balloon test, the string round the warm yeast balloon measured 30 cm. The string round the no-yeast balloon measured 10 cm. How many times bigger round was the yeast balloon?
maths.explain: The yeast balloon was 30 cm round. The no-yeast balloon was 10 cm round. 30 divided by 10 is 3. So the yeast balloon was 3 times as big round. You can check: 10 + 10 + 10 = 30.

chart.title: Distance round each balloon after 30 minutes (made-up example)

maths.context: This is about the balloon test, where you put dried yeast in warm sugar water with a balloon on top, next to a bottle with no yeast.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'three times bigger' tells us how strong the effect of the living yeast was, compared with the bottle without it.

maths.problem: In the candle trial, you tested the flame against 9 signs of life. It showed 5 of them: moving, using fuel, using air, growing and making waste. How many signs did it not show?
maths.explain: There were 9 signs in all. The flame showed 5. 9 take away 5 is 4. The 4 it did not show included being made of cells and passing on instructions. Those are the ones that matter most.
maths.context: This is about the candle trial, where a grown-up lit a candle and you tested the flame against each sign of life.
maths.why_maths: Counting the signs a thing shows and lacks helps us compare tricky cases fairly, instead of guessing.

maths.problem: In the crystal garden, the biggest crystal was 2 mm on day 3, 4 mm on day 5 and 6 mm on day 7. If it keeps growing the same way, how big will it be on day 9?
maths.explain: Every two days, the crystal grew 2 mm: 2, then 4, then 6. The pattern adds 2 each time. So on day 9 it will be 6 + 2 = 8 mm. In real life the crystal will stop when the water dries up or the salt runs out.
maths.context: This is about the crystal garden, where salt crystals grew on a thread hanging in salty water, and you measured the biggest one.
maths.why_maths: Finding a pattern in measurements lets scientists predict what will happen next, and then test whether they were right.

roots.context: We have been putting tricky cases on trial: fire, crystals, robots, sleeping seeds, water bears and viruses. Now we ask what these puzzles tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Life does not begin where we draw the line. The edge between alive and not alive is drawn by us, not by nature.
deep_truth.habit: We sort the world into two boxes, alive and not alive, as if nature made the boxes. But a dry seed, a tun and a virus sit between them. The boxes are our words, and the world is smoother than our words.
deep_truth.evidence: A dry seed shows no signs of life and is alive. A flame shows many signs and is not. A virus is lifeless outside a cell and busy inside one.

three.who_am_i: You are made of the same atoms as rocks, air and stars. About 8 out of every 100 parts of your instructions came from viruses long ago.
three.what_is_life: Life is not a special stuff. It is ordinary atoms, arranged and kept busy, like a flame that knows how to keep itself going.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is not split cleanly into living and non-living. There are sleepers, waiters and in-betweens everywhere.

roots.thread: Everything in a seed, a flame and you is made of the same few kinds of atoms. DeepKids believes this is the One showing up as many things. Some of those things are arranged to stay busy, repair themselves and pass on instructions, and we call them alive. Others rest, like a seed, and some only borrow life, like a virus. The many look sharply different, but underneath they shade into each other.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to break open a tiny banyan seed. 'What do you see?' 'Nothing at all.' The father says: from this nothing that you cannot see, the whole great banyan tree grows.
teachings.link: A dry seed looks like nothing is happening inside it. Yet a whole living tree waits there, resting.

teachings.teaching: The Greek thinker Heraclitus said the world is like an ever-living fire, always burning and always changing, yet keeping its pattern.
teachings.link: A flame and a living body both keep their shape while new stuff flows through them. That is why fire is such a tricky case, and why life is so hard to define.

teachings.teaching: The hymn of creation asks how everything began, and ends with an honest question: perhaps even the one who watches from the highest heaven does not know.
teachings.link: Scientists still do not know how the first life came from non-living things. Saying 'we do not know' is part of being honest.

science.text: Living things are made of the same kinds of atoms as non-living things, and most of those atoms were made in stars.
How the very first life came from non-living chemicals is not known. There are ideas, like the RNA idea, and experiments, but no answer yet.

other_view.view: The line is not just our words. Cells and inherited instructions are a real difference in nature. Fire and crystals really lack them. A few in-between cases do not mean there is no line, just as dusk does not mean day and night are the same.

practice.title: The sleeping seed
practice.say: Let's be a seed. Curl up small on the floor, and hold one dry seed in your hand. Breathe in slowly. Breathe out slowly. Make your breath so small and quiet that you almost cannot feel it, like a resting seed. Stay very still while I count to twenty. Now imagine warm rain falling on you. Slowly, slowly, uncurl. Stretch one arm up like a shoot. Open your eyes. Were you alive the whole time you were still?
practice.kid: Curl up small, holding a dry seed. Breathe very slowly and quietly. Stay still while you count to twenty. Now imagine warm rain. Slowly uncurl and stretch up like a shoot.

ask: When you are fast asleep, how do you know you are still alive?
Is there anything in the world that is completely not alive? How could you be sure?
If the line between alive and not alive is drawn by people, who should get to draw it?
Part of you came from viruses long ago. Where do you end and the rest of the world begin?
